title: A Alibi for the Verdict
premise: When the coffin of Harlan Voss, founder of the town of Meridian Falls, is found empty during a cemetery relocation, night-shift taxi dispatcher August Pemberton realizes the dispatch logs they've archived for seven years contain calls that shouldn't exist—pickups from the Voss mausoleum dated decades before August was hired. Following the paper trail, August discovers that a cab company has been quietly ferrying a living Harlan Voss between safe houses for thirty years, and that their own predecessor dispatcher vanished rather than keep lying. The alibi network was built by the town's founding families to hide the fact that Voss faked his death to escape embezzlement charges, and every loyal member of it is now a suspect in his actual murder—committed three weeks ago when someone finally learned the truth. August must choose between protecting the found family of drivers who raised them and exposing the verdict the town already delivered; in the end, August testifies with the logs, sending one driver to prison but freeing the rest, and learns that loyalty and truth can share a grave only if you dig it yourself.
about_author: Paloma Whitlock spent a decade answering late-night phones for a regional transit authority, where she collected the strange confessions strangers make when they think no one is listening. She writes mysteries about small towns and the people paid to know everything and say nothing.

chapters.title: The Empty Man
chapters.summary: POV: August Pemberton. When workers relocating the Voss mausoleum find the founder's coffin empty, the town erupts in speculation—and August recognizes the exhumation date as one circled in an old dispatch ledger they inherited. Digging into the archive, they find recurring midnight pickups logged at the cemetery across three decades, all signed off by a dispatcher who vanished in 1998. Emotional beat: the quiet dread of realizing your tidy, invisible life is built on someone else's buried secret.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Fares
chapters.summary: POV: August. Reconstructing the route map, August traces the pickups to a shuttered lake house and finds evidence Harlan Voss lived there until recently—then died there, three weeks ago, and someone drove the body away. The senior drivers close ranks, feeding August warm lies about 'company history,' and August understands the cab company itself is the alibi machine. Emotional beat: the ache of suspecting the people who fed you soup on bad nights.

chapters.title: Every Alibi Has a Driver
chapters.summary: POV: August. Confronted by matriarch driver Ruth Calloway, August learns the whole truth: the founding families funded Voss's disappearance, and the statute expires in nine days—after which the cover-up becomes conspiracy. But the murder breaks the pact: one driver killed Voss to stop him from blackmailing the families, and Ruth knows which one. Emotional beat: rising panic as loyalty curdles into complicity, and the clock starts running.

chapters.title: What the Verdict Weighs
chapters.summary: POV: August. At the county courthouse, with the statute hours from expiring, August surrenders the full dispatch archive, naming the killer—the gentle driver who taught them the radio codes—while shielding the rest under a negotiated plea. The town's beloved founder is posthumously disgraced, the cab company survives under new ownership, and August takes the dispatcher's chair permanently, no longer invisible but no longer alone. Emotional beat: grief braided with relief—the costly peace of choosing truth without abandoning family.
